title: The Specific Way the Enemy Attacks People Who Are Close to Their Breakthrough
fullText: The night before Israel crossed the Red Sea, Pharaoh changed his mind and sent his entire army after them. The morning before Joseph walked into Pharaoh's throne room as prime minister, he woke up as a prisoner. The day before Elijah's greatest victory at Mount Carmel, he was in hiding, convinced he was the only one left. In every single one of these stories, the most intense attack came closest to the breakthrough. Not randomly, not coincidentally. The pattern is too consistent across too many centuries and too many different people for it to be accidental. I want to make something clear before we go further. This video is not about blaming the enemy for every hard thing in your life. Not every difficulty is spiritual warfare. Some things are just life. Some things are consequences. Some things are God's own doing. But there is a specific category of attack, a specific cluster of tactics that appear again and again in scripture, always in the same window of time, right before something significant is about to happen. And if you don't recognize them, you will respond to them as though they're just circumstances. You will make decisions based on what you feel instead of what is actually happening. And you will walk away from the door the moment before it opened. Here are the four ways the enemy attacks people who are close to their breakthrough. And more importantly, how to recognize each one when it's happening to you. Before the tactics, I need you to understand the strategy behind them. Because once you see the strategy, the tactics make complete sense. The enemy is not trying to destroy you. Destruction would be too obvious. What he is trying to do is much more precise. He is trying to get you to disqualify yourself, to walk away, to give up one step before the door opens. Because if you walk away voluntarily, he doesn't have to fight you in the assignment God has prepared for you. Job 1 is the clearest window into how this works. When God pointed out Job to the enemy and said, "Have you considered my servant Job? There is no one on earth like him." The enemy didn't immediately destroy Job. He asked permission. He proposed a series of escalating tests designed to make Job curse God and walk away from his faith on his own terms. The goal was not annihilation. It was resignation. That is still the goal. Not to crush you from the outside, to wear you down from the inside until you make the decision yourself. And this is why the attacks almost always feel internal, like your own thoughts, like your own emotions, like your own discouragement. Because the enemy knows that a wound you inflict on yourself is always deeper than one he could inflict directly. With that in mind, here are the four specific tactics. The first tactic is the one most people never recognize because it looks exactly like a natural consequence. It is the sudden arrival of total exhaustion, physical, emotional, and spiritual, at the precise moment when you need your strength the most. Elijah is the most striking example of this in all of scripture and his story needs to be understood in its full sequence to grasp what was actually happening. First Kings chapter 18 records one of the greatest single days in the Old Testament. Elijah stood alone against 450 prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel. He called down fire from heaven. He proved beyond any question that the God of Israel was the living God. The people fell on their faces and cried out, "The Lord, he is God. The Lord, he is God." 450 false prophets were executed. And then, because it still wasn't raining, Elijah climbed to the top of the mountain and prayed seven times until a cloud the size of a man's hand appeared on the horizon. He told Ahab to get in his chariot before the rain stopped him. And then scripture records that the hand of the Lord was on Elijah and he ran ahead of Ahab's chariot to Jezrael. He outran a chariot on foot for 20 miles. That is the high point. One of the most dramatic victories in the entire Bible. And then Jezebel sent a message. One sentence. By this time tomorrow, you will be dead just like those prophets. Elijah's response, he fled. He ran more than a 100 miles to Beeba. He went a day's journey into the desert alone. And he sat under a broom tree and said, "It is enough, Lord. Take my life. I am no better than my ancestors." The man who had just called down fire from heaven asked God to let him die. Now, here is what most people miss when they read this story. They ask, "How could Elijah collapse so completely, so fast after such an enormous victory?" The answer is physical. He had spent enormous energy on Mount Carmel. He had run 20 m in the rain. He was physically depleted in a way that left him emotionally and spiritually undefended. And Jezebel's threat, which was probably a tactical move, not a sincere promise. If she had truly wanted him dead, she would have simply sent soldiers. Not a warning landed in the exact moment when he had nothing left to resist it with. The enemy knows when you're depleted. He knows when the adrenaline of a spiritual high has worn off. He knows when you've given everything and have no reserves left, and that is the moment he applies pressure. God's response to Elijah in this state is worth noting carefully. He did not rebuke him. He did not tell him to pull himself together. An angel showed up, touched him, and said, "Arise and eat. The journey is too great for you." He let Elijah sleep. He gave him bread and water twice. He treated the exhaustion as what it was, a physical and emotional reality that needed to be addressed before anything spiritual could be spoken. If you are in a season where you feel completely emptied out at exactly the moment you needed to be strong, recognize what that is. It is not weakness of faith. It may be the enemy applying pressure at your most vulnerable point. The response is not to push harder. It is to do what Elijah did. Rest, eat, and wait for the angel's second touch before you move. Tactic two, conflict in the closest relationship right before the mission launches. The second tactic is relational. And it is perhaps the most disorienting because it comes from someone you trust, not from someone you'd expect an attack from. Paul and Barnabas had been together for years. They had traveled together, suffered together, been sent out by the Holy Spirit together, established churches together, defended the gospel together at the Jerusalem Council. They were the most proven missionary partnership in the early church. And in Acts 15, right at the moment, they were about to launch the second missionary journey. The journey that would bring the gospel to Europe for the first time. They had what scripture calls a sharp disagreement. The Greek word Luke uses is paroxismos, a word that conveys a sharp eruption of contention, an intense clash. It was so severe that they separated. Two men who had shared every hardship of the first journey could not resolve a disagreement about John Mark in time to leave together. Now, here is what I want you to see. If Paul and Barnabas had stayed together and resolved the disagreement, one team would have gone out. Because they separated, two teams went out, each carrying the gospel to different regions simultaneously. What looked like the catastrophic collapse of the most effective missionary partnership in the church, doubled the missionary reach. The enemy probably intended the conflict to stop the mission entirely. God used it to multiply the mission. But here's what Paul and Barnabas would have felt in the moment of that conflict. Not multiplication, not divine strategy, not expansion. They would have felt the pain of division between people who had shared everything. They would have felt the grief of a friendship fractured at the worst possible time. This is the nature of the second tactic. It is not designed to feel like warfare. It is designed to feel like a very painful relational breakdown at a very inconvenient moment. It creates confusion, grief, and self-doubt. It makes you question whether the mission was right if even the people closest to it can't stay together. If you are experiencing significant relational conflict right now, especially conflict with someone who has been a partner in what God has called you to pay attention to the timing, ask whether this conflict, if handled with integrity, might actually produce something larger than what you had before. Not every conflict is the enemy, but conflict arriving right at the threshold of a significant season is worth examining more carefully than conflict that arrives in a quiet moment. Tactic three, whispers of inadequacy right before confirmation arrives. The third tactic is the most internal and the most dangerous because it sounds almost exactly like the voice of wisdom and self-awareness. When Peter had been fishing all night and caught nothing, Jesus told him to put his nets out into the deep. And Peter's response before he obeyed was, "Master, we have worked hard all night and haven't caught anything." That was not doubt. That was honest exhaustion. He rode to the deep and let the nets down anyway, and the catch nearly sank two boats. But there is another Peter moment that illustrates the third tactic more precisely. In Luke 5, when the nets came up full and the catch overwhelmed the boats, Peter's response was not celebration. He fell at Jesus's knees and said, "Go away from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man." In the moment of the greatest confirmation of his calling, two boats full of fish. The physical proof of divine favor, his immediate reaction was, "I don't deserve this. I shouldn't be here. Get away from me." Jesus's response was immediate. Do not be afraid. From now on, you will be catching people. That is the pattern. Right before major confirmation arrives, there is often a surge of the opposite. A wave of feeling completely unqualified, completely exposed, completely out of your depth. And if you trust that feeling more than you trust the evidence of what God has already done, you will disqualify yourself from what he was about to give you. Now there is a critical distinction that determines everything about how you respond to this tactic and it is the distinction between conviction and condemnation. Conviction is the Holy Spirit telling you something specific that needs to change with a clear path toward change. It points you toward God. It says here is the issue. Here is the correction. Now move toward me. Conviction is specific, purposeful, and produces repentance that leads to freedom. Condemnation is the enemy telling you that you are fundamentally unworthy without specifying anything actionable. It points you away from God. It says you are a failure. You don't deserve this. God is done with you. Condemnation is vague, crushing, and produces shame that leads to hiding. Romans 8:1 is unambiguous. There is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. That sentence is a theological statement, but it is also a discernment tool. If the voice in your head is condemning you in ways that match that description, vague shame, a sense of being fundamentally unworthy, an impulse to withdraw that voice is not from the one who said there is no condemnation. And Revelation 12:10 names it plainly. The enemy is the accuser of the brethren who accuses them day and night. Accusation is his primary tactic, not fire, not earthquake accusation. And if he can make the accusation loud enough and frequent enough in the exact moment before your confirmation arrives, he can get you to walk away before you receive what was being given to you. The diagnostic is straightforward. Does the voice you're hearing make you want to run toward God or away from him? Conviction draws you toward him? Condemnation pushes you away? That is the difference between the Holy Spirit and the accuser. And knowing the difference in real time may be the most practically important skill in your spiritual life. Tactic four, making the final step look like the wrong direction. The fourth tactic is the most dramatic. It is the moment right before the door opens when everything resets to look like the worst possible outcome. The circumstances arranged themselves to appear to say, "This was wrong from the beginning. Go back." Moses at the Red Sea is the clearest image. Israel had left Egypt. The plagues were over. Pharaoh had released them. They were out free for the first time in 400 years. And then Pharaoh changed his mind. The Egyptian army appeared behind them. The Red Sea was in front of them. And the people turned on Moses with language that reveals exactly what this tactic is designed to produce. Was it because there were no graves in Egypt that you brought us to the desert to die? Didn't we say to you in Egypt, "Leave us alone. Let us serve the Egyptians. It would have been better for us to serve the Egyptians than to die in the desert." In that moment, going back to Egypt felt like the rational choice. It felt safer. It felt like what should have been done from the beginning. The final tactic doesn't just create fear. It creates revision. It makes the entire journey look like a mistake. God's instruction to Moses in that moment is the operating principle for every person facing the fourth tactic. He said, "Do not be afraid. Stand firm and you will see the deliverance the Lord will bring you today and then the Lord will fight for you. You need only to be still. Stand firm. Be still. The crossing requires forward movement. But before the water parted, the instruction was stillness, not retreat, not a new plan, not a conversation about whether Egypt was actually better. stillness and trust that what God promised does not get cancelled by what circumstances appear to say in the final hour before it happens. This is the final tactic because it is the final test. It is the enemy's last opportunity to get you to reverse direction before the door opens. Everything before this was about slowing you down, exhaustion, conflict, accusation. This last tactic is about reversal, about making forward look like backward, about making the promise look like the mistake. The people who crossed the Red Sea were not the ones who had perfect faith throughout the journey. They were the ones who did not turn around when the army appeared behind them. That is the standard. Not perfect faith. Just don't turn around. I need to say something carefully before I close. Not every hard thing is an attack. Not every exhaustion means breakthrough is near. Not every conflict is spiritual warfare. God himself sometimes allows difficulty not as a sign of proximity to breakthrough but as a season of formation, discipline or redirection. So I am not telling you to interpret every painful thing as evidence that you're close to something great. That kind of thinking produces spiritual arrogance. The belief that your suffering is always the enemy's attack and therefore always a sign of your importance. What I am saying is this. There is a specific pattern in scripture that is worth recognizing. exhaustion, relational conflict, internal accusation, and circumstances that appear to reverse the promise arriving together in close proximity. In a season where God has been moving, that pattern is worth paying attention to, not to produce pride, but to produce discernment, and discernment produces steadiness instead of panic. After Elijah sat under the broom tree and asked God to let him die, the angel touched him a second time and said, "Arise and eat, for the journey is too great for you." The journey is too great for you. Not the journey is too great. Full stop. The journey is too great for you. Meaning for you on your own in your current condition without rest, without provision, without being touched again. God did not cancel the journey. He fed him for it. After Paul and Barnabas separated, Paul took Silas and they went through Syria and Cissia. They eventually reached Macedonia. And the first convert in Europe was a woman named Lydia, a dealer in purple cloth, whose heart the Lord opened to respond to Paul's message. The conflict that looked like the end of the mission opened a continent. After Moses stretched out his staff over the Red Sea and the waters parted, Israel walked through on dry ground. The Egyptian army followed and was swallowed by the returning water. And on the other side, Moses and all of Israel sang. The breakthrough came every time. Not because the attacks weren't real. Not because the people weren't genuinely afraid and depleted and conflicted and confused, but because they did not turn around in the final hour. You may be in one of these four attacks right now. Exhausted at the worst moment, in unexpected conflict with someone you trusted, hearing the accuser's voice louder than you've ever heard it, or standing at something that looks from every angle like the wrong direction. The question is not whether the attack is real. It probably is. The question is whether you will stand firm long enough to see what was on the other side of it all along.
